subject: maths
title: Forming expressions from words and patterns

scenes.heading: Forming expressions
scenes.sub: From words and patterns to algebra
scenes.say: How many matchsticks do you need for fifty squares in a row? You could count, or you could write one expression that answers it for any number of squares. Let's learn how.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.science: "5 less than x" becomes x − 5: the order flips
scenes.breaks: Everyday words can mean several things; an algebraic expression has exactly one meaning.
scenes.say: Writing algebra from words is like translating into another language. You cannot always go word by word. Five less than x becomes x minus five, with the order flipped.
scenes.caption: Writing algebra from words is like translating into another language. You cannot always go word by word. "5 less than x" becomes x − 5, with the order flipped.

scenes.heading: Order and brackets
scenes.say: Seven less than three n is three n minus seven. When words group things, like the sum of n and five, times four, use brackets. And three numbers in a row are n, n plus one and n plus two.
scenes.caption: 7 less than 3n is 3n − 7. When words group things, like "the sum of n and 5, times 4", use brackets: 4(n + 5). Three numbers in a row are n, n + 1 and n + 2.

scenes.heading: A growing pattern
notes: One stick to start, then 3 per square
scenes.say: Here are matchstick squares in a row. Shape one has four sticks, shape two has seven, shape three has ten. Each new square adds three sticks, plus there is one starting stick. So the rule is three n plus one.
scenes.caption: Matchstick squares: 4, 7, 10 sticks. Each new square adds 3 sticks, plus one starting stick. So the rule is 3n + 1.

scenes.heading: Rule for a linear pattern
scenes.say: For any pattern that goes up by the same amount, multiply n by the common difference, then add the first term minus the difference. For four, seven, ten, that is three n plus one.
scenes.caption: For a pattern that goes up by the same amount: d × n + (first term − d). For 4, 7, 10: 3n + 1.

scenes.heading: Which shape uses 100 sticks?
scenes.question: Matchstick squares: rule 3n + 1. Which shape uses exactly 100 sticks?
scenes.say: Which shape uses one hundred sticks? Set three n plus one equal to one hundred. Take away one: three n is ninety-nine. Divide by three: shape thirty-three.
scenes.caption: Which shape uses 100 sticks? 3n + 1 = 100. Take away 1: 3n = 99. Divide by 3: shape 33.

scenes.heading: Explain why
scenes.question: Why is the sum of three consecutive whole numbers always a multiple of 3?
scenes.say: Why is the sum of three numbers in a row always a multiple of three? Add n, n plus one and n plus two to get three n plus three. That is three times n plus one, so it is always a multiple of three.
scenes.caption: Add n, n + 1 and n + 2 to get 3n + 3 = 3(n + 1). That is always 3 × a whole number, so always a multiple of 3.

scenes.say: Quick recap. Less than flips the order. Grouped words need brackets. Consecutive numbers are n, n plus one, n plus two. A pattern rule is the difference times n, plus the first term minus the difference. Check with two cases. Now try the practice questions!
